729.title: The hidden gift
729.hook: Zhuangzi's hunchback Shu is spared the army and fed by the state (Zhuangzi 4)
729.carry: a side the world's measuring stick misses
729.howItsDone: Readers of the Zhuangzi, Daoists among them, read Shu and the useless tree together as stories about the use of the useless, and some return to them in times of illness, disability or failure.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hukam, the order no one is outside of. Your line was no one is outside it.

The recruiters have come to town, rounding up men for the army, and every young man with a strong back has found somewhere to hide: the hayloft, an aunt's house, the reeds by the river. Except one. He's strolling down the middle of the street, arms swinging, saying hello to the officers. Nobody stops him. Nobody looks twice. His name, in the book of Zhuangzi, is Shu, and the reason nobody drafts him is his body.
screen: `THE RECRUITERS COME TO TOWN.` → `EVERYONE HIDES. EXCEPT ONE.` → `HIS NAME IS SHU.`

segments.voice: First, who Shu is. Zhuangzi draws him in big, almost cartoon strokes: his chin tucked down by his navel, his shoulders higher than the top of his head, his hair knot pointing at the sky. A body that fits none of the world's measures. Second, how he lives. He isn't helpless in the story. He earns his food sewing and washing clothes, and by sifting grain he makes enough to feed others besides himself. Third, the turn. When the army comes, he walks among the recruiters without fear. When the state calls up men for heavy labor, he's excused because of his condition. When it hands out grain to the sick, he gets his share, and firewood too. Then Zhuangzi draws the lesson, in paraphrase: if a man whose body is out of the usual shape can look after himself and live out his years, how much more someone whose virtue is out of the usual shape. The chapter is set in a dangerous world, where being useful gets you used up. This path met the useless tree in its first year; Shu is its neighbor in the same chapter, which ends, in paraphrase: everyone knows the use of the useful, but nobody knows the use of the useless. Fourth, what it isn't. Zhuangzi doesn't say every limit is secretly a blessing, and nobody gets to tell you yours is. He turns the picture once, to show a side the world's measuring stick misses. The gift is hidden, partial, and still real.
screen: `A BODY THAT FITS NO MEASURE.` · `HE EARNS HIS KEEP.` · `SPARED THE ARMY, FED BY THE STATE.` · `NOT A PROMISE. A TURNED PICTURE.` · then, large: `THE USE OF THE USELESS.`

segments.voice: Let one limit you live with come to mind, small enough to hold today: a knee that won't run, a shyness, no car, not enough money for what everyone else is doing. Hold it without arguing, and ask it two quiet questions: what do you spare me from, and what do you leave room for? Maybe something comes, a slower walk where you notice more; maybe nothing does, and that's an honest answer too.
Shu, the man in Zhuangzi whose body didn't fit the world's measure, and who was spared and fed because of it. Today's word.
Your line: a side the world's measuring stick misses. Zhuangzi turns the picture once, and lets you look. Day seven hundred twenty-nine, done.

730.title: All shall be well
730.hook: Julian is told that all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well (Revelations of Divine Love 27)
730.howItsDone: Christians of several churches read Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love, and her line all shall be well is sometimes said or sung in prayer services and at times of grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Shu, spared because his body fit none of the world's measures. Your line was a side the world's measuring stick misses.
screen: `A SIDE THE WORLD'S MEASURING STICK MISSES.`

segments.voice: All shall be well. Said fast, it can sound like it'll be fine, something said over a shoulder on the way out of a room. But the woman who wrote it down heard it in her sickbed. Julian of Norwich, whom this path met with a hazelnut in her palm, writes that she was so ill the people around her thought she was dying. And she wasn't asking for comfort. She was asking a hard question.
screen: `SAID FAST, IT SOUNDS LIKE: IT'LL BE FINE.` → `JULIAN HEARD IT IN THE BED.` → `SHE WAS ASKING A HARD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the question. In chapter twenty-seven of her Revelations of Divine Love, Julian says she wondered why God, in all his foreseeing wisdom, didn't stop sin at the very beginning. Then, she thought, all would have been well. It's the old why, asked straight, by someone in pain. Second, the answer. She doesn't get a reason. She hears that sin was behovely, an old word for fitting, something that had its place. And then the line, in Grace Warrack's edition: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Third, the tone. In her telling, the words came very tenderly, with no blame laid on her, nor on any who shall be saved. Not a lecture, not a correction for asking. A promise, said kindly to a person who had dared the question. Fourth, the tense. Shall. Not all is well: all shall be. Julian doesn't pretend the world in front of her is fine, and she doesn't stop asking. In the chapters that follow she keeps pressing how it could ever be made well, with so much harm in the world. Later she is told, in paraphrase, that she'll see it herself: that all manner of thing shall be well. So the line doesn't end the question. It's a promise that keeps her company while the question stays open. Some Christians who read Julian hold it that way; some readers take it simply as a line from a woman who asked honestly, and was answered gently.

segments.voice: Let one thing that isn't well right now come to mind, yours or someone else's. Then, once, silently and slowly, say Julian's line, sin was behovely, without repeating it to drown the hard thing out, and notice how it lands. If it rings true, let it; if it rings false today, let that be honest too; if you pray, offer it as a promise; if not, hold it as a line from a book.
Julian, the medieval mystic who asked God why sin wasn't stopped at the start, and was answered not with a reason but a promise. Today's word.
Your line: sin was behovely. A promise, while the question stays open. See you tomorrow.

731.title: Ivan's rebellion
731.hook: in Dostoevsky, Ivan refuses a harmony bought with a child's tears (The Brothers Karamazov, book 5)
731.howItsDone: Readers, believers and unbelievers alike, return to Ivan's chapter when they think about the problem of suffering, and it's read in literature, philosophy and theology classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Julian, sick in bed, asking why and hearing a tender promise. Your line was sin was behovely.

A small-town tavern, and two brothers at a table. The younger, Alyosha, is a novice at the local monastery, gentle, a listener. The older, Ivan, is brilliant and restless, and tonight he says out loud what he really thinks. He's been collecting things, he tells his brother: clippings, stories. And he isn't going to argue about whether God exists. He's going to argue about something harder. This is Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, and the chapter is called Rebellion.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS IN A TAVERN.` → `IVAN HAS BEEN COLLECTING THINGS.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED REBELLION.`

segments.voice: First, the collection. Ivan has been gathering true stories of cruelty done to children. He tells several. They're too hard to repeat here, and that's his point. The grown-ups, he says, have eaten the apple, so to speak; let them answer for it. But the children haven't. Why should they suffer? Second, the refusal. Ivan imagines the end of everything: every wrong explained, everyone embracing, a harmony where all is made right. And he doesn't want it, if it costs one child's tears. It isn't worth that price. He's careful: it isn't God he refuses, he says. He just, most respectfully, returns his ticket. Alyosha quietly names it: that's rebellion. Third, the question. Ivan turns it on his brother. Suppose you were building the world, to make people happy at last, and it could only be done by torturing one small child. Would you agree to be the builder on those terms? Tell the truth. And Alyosha, the novice, answers softly: no, I wouldn't consent. Fourth, what the book does next. Alyosha doesn't win the argument. He speaks of one who can forgive everything, because he gave his own innocent blood. Ivan answers with a long poem about a Grand Inquisitor. When it ends, Alyosha doesn't rebut it. He leans over and kisses his brother. Dostoevsky lets the question stand at full strength, in the mouth of a character he gave strong arguments. This block has listened to Job, the cross, the Quran's patience, Julian's promise. Ivan is the voice that says: not at that price. The novel gives him his full say, and so does this day.
screen: `STORIES OF CHILDREN WHO SUFFERED.` · `I RETURN MY TICKET.` · `WOULD YOU BUILD IT ON ONE CHILD?` · `A KISS, NOT A REBUTTAL.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION STAYS.`

segments.voice: Pick one hard question you can't answer, one you can hold for two minutes: why that happened to them, why it goes on. Hold it like a stone in your open hand, and each time the mind reaches for an answer or for the exit, notice, and set the question gently back in your palm. You're not solving it, only letting it be a real question, as the brothers did at that table.
Ivan's rebellion. In The Brothers Karamazov, his refusal of any harmony bought with a child's tears. A question the novel lets stand. Today's word.
Your line: the question stays. Some questions deserve to be held, not hurried. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

732.title: Meaning, even here
732.hook: Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist who was held in the Nazi camps, argued meaning can be found even in suffering (Man's Search for Meaning)
732.howItsDone: Frankl's approach, which he called logotherapy, is taught in some counseling and psychotherapy training, and his book is read by people facing grief, illness and loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Ivan's rebellion: a ticket returned, and Alyosha's answer, a kiss. Your line was the question stays.

An older doctor comes to see a psychiatrist. His wife has died, and he can't get out from under the grief. He loved her above everything, he says. The psychiatrist doesn't offer advice. He asks a question instead: what would have happened if you had died first, and she had been left to go on without you? The man answers: for her, that would have been terrible. How she would have suffered. The psychiatrist was Viktor Frankl, and he tells this story in Man's Search for Meaning.
screen: `AN OLDER DOCTOR, GRIEVING.` → `WHAT IF YOU HAD DIED FIRST?` → `HOW SHE WOULD HAVE SUFFERED.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. Frankl answers, in paraphrase: you see, she was spared that suffering, and it was you who spared her, at the price of surviving her and mourning her. The man says nothing more. He shakes Frankl's hand and leaves. Nothing about the loss has changed; the grief is still there. But, Frankl writes, it now had a meaning: a sacrifice made for her. Second, where Frankl learned this. He had been a prisoner in the Nazi camps, Auschwitz among them, and the first part of his book is his plain account of that time. Not a hero story: hunger, cold, and what he saw people do, the worst and the best. Third, the claim. Frankl names ways a person finds meaning: by doing a deed or making something, by loving someone or experiencing something, and, when suffering can't be avoided, by the stance a person takes toward it. That third way is today's. Fourth, what he doesn't say. Suffering isn't needed for meaning, he says. If suffering can be avoided, the meaningful thing is to remove it, whether the cause or the pain. Choosing pain you don't have to bear isn't heroic, in his words; it's just needless. Meaning is not the reason something hard happens. It's something a person can still find, or make, inside it. And no one gets to hand it to someone else. The doctor found his own, in answer to a question.
screen: `YOU SPARED HER THAT.` · `A PRISONER IN THE CAMPS.` · `DEED, LOVE, AND THE STANCE YOU TAKE.` · `IF YOU CAN END IT, END IT.` · then, large: `MEANING, EVEN HERE.`

segments.voice: Choose one hard thing in your life you can hold, a caregiving season, a job you can't leave yet, a loss, and gently ask it Frankl's kind of question: who is this for, and what could it make possible, even something small? If an answer comes, let it be modest; if none comes, that's allowed, and the question can wait.
Meaning. For Frankl, what a person can still find in deeds, in love, and, when suffering can't be avoided, in how they bear it. Not the reason for the pain. Today's word.
Your line: a sacrifice made for her. The grief stayed; what changed was its meaning. That's day seven hundred thirty-two.

733.title: The last freedom
733.hook: Frankl: the freedom to choose one's attitude can't be taken (Man's Search for Meaning)
733.howItsDone: Readers of Frankl, and some counselors trained in his logotherapy, practice noticing the space between what happens and how they respond, and choosing a stance toward what they can't change.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was meaning: the grieving doctor, and a loss that became a sacrifice. Your line was a sacrifice made for her.

Evening, in a prisoners' hut. Everyone is starving. The daily ration is a little bread and thin soup, and every crumb counts. And Frankl remembers men who walked through the huts comforting others, and giving away their last piece of bread. There may have been few of them, he says. But they were there. And for him, that was proof of something. Not about how strong they were. About what can and can't be taken from a person.
screen: `EVENING IN A PRISONERS' HUT.` → `MEN WHO GAVE AWAY THEIR LAST BREAD.` → `WHAT CAN'T BE TAKEN?`

segments.voice: First, what was taken. Frankl's account of the camps is a list of losses: his name replaced by a number, his clothes, his hair, his manuscript, and no knowledge of whether the people he loved were alive. Everything a person usually leans on, gone. Second, what wasn't. From watching those men in the huts, Frankl draws his conclusion, in paraphrase: everything can be taken from a person but one thing, the last of the human freedoms, to choose one's attitude in any given circumstances, to choose one's own way. Third, how small it can be. In his account, this freedom isn't a grand speech. It's a shared crust, a kind word to the man in the next bunk. Once, marching in the cold, Frankl kept himself going by picturing himself in a warm lecture hall, describing the camp as something to be studied. That was his own way: turning toward the suffering as something to understand, not only to endure. Fourth, what it isn't. This is not a grade for anyone in pain. Frankl writes as a witness, not a judge, and the freedom he describes is a door that's there, not a test some people fail. Nor does it excuse anyone who causes suffering. The camps were a crime; the freedom he found inside them doesn't make them less of one. It means that even there, one small choice was still a person's own: the stance they took toward what was happening.

734.title: Water at the pump
734.hook: water on one hand, the word spelled into the other, and Helen Keller's locked world opens (The Story of My Life, 4)
734.howItsDone: Readers come back to Helen Keller's account of the well house when they think about language, teaching and breakthrough, and the scene is retold in schools and on stage.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Frankl, and the men who gave away their last bread. Your line was my attitude.

A broken doll lies on the floor by the hearth. The girl who smashed it feels nothing about it, she later writes: no sorrow, no regret. She can't see and she can't hear, and her teacher has been spelling words into her hand day after day, letters pressed into the palm with quick fingers. The girl can copy the shapes. She has no idea they mean anything. So her teacher takes her out into the warm day, down the path to the well house, where someone is drawing water at the pump.
screen: `A BROKEN DOLL BY THE HEARTH.` → `LETTERS PRESSED INTO A PALM.` → `DOWN THE PATH TO THE PUMP.`

segments.voice: First, the two hands. This is Helen Keller's own account, in chapter four of The Story of My Life. Her teacher, Anne Sullivan, puts one of Helen's hands under the spout. Cool water rushes over it. Into the other hand she spells w-a-t-e-r, slowly at first, then fast. Helen stands still, all her attention on those moving fingers. Second, the opening. Something like a forgotten memory stirs, she writes, and the mystery of language comes open. In her words: "I knew then that 'w-a-t-e-r' meant the wonderful cool something that was flowing over my hand." Not a shape in the palm: a name for a thing. And if this had a name, everything did. Third, the doll. On the way back to the house, she writes, every object she touched seemed alive. She remembers the doll she broke, feels her way to the hearth, picks up the pieces, and tries, uselessly, to put them together. Now her eyes filled with tears. She understood what she had done, and she was sorry. A word for water, and then a word for wrong. Fourth, why it's here, in a block on suffering. Her account doesn't say the dark and the silence went away. They didn't. What changed was that she was no longer alone inside them. Someone had reached in with a name, and a word became a bridge between two people. She calls it a living word, one that set her soul free. Not a cure. A way through.

735.title: No ranking
735.hook: the voices of this block keep company with pain; none of them asks anyone to rank it or compare it to someone else's
735.howItsDone: In Jewish mourning, visitors to a shiva house may wait for the mourner to speak first, and Christians read Romans 12:15 as a call to share both joy and grief; some chaplains and counselors are taught not to compare one person's pain with another's.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Helen Keller at the pump, water on one hand and the word in the other. Your line was water.

"At least it's not cancer." "Other people have it so much worse." "I shouldn't complain, after what she's been through." These lines get said with the best intentions, sometimes to a friend, often to ourselves. They sound humble. But listen to what they do. They put pain on a scale, and somebody's pain has to lose. Across this whole block, from Job to Julian to Frankl, the texts keep company with suffering in many ways. They don't line it up and rank it.
screen: `AT LEAST IT'S NOT...` → `PAIN ON A SCALE.` → `SOMEBODY ALWAYS LOSES.`

segments.voice: First, Job's friends, at their best. When they arrive, the King James Bible says: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." They didn't measure it against anyone's. They sat in it with him. It's when they start explaining and weighing that the book turns against them. Second, Paul, to the church in Rome: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Weep with, not weigh against. Paul sets it in a list of ways to live alongside each other. Third, Frankl, a man who had every reason to rank. In Man's Search for Meaning he offers a picture, in paraphrase: suffering behaves like a gas in an empty room. A little gas or a lot, it fills the whole room. So a person's suffering, great or small, fills the whole of them. The size of suffering, he says, is relative, and comparing doesn't shrink anything. Fourth, the week. Shu showed a gift the world's measure missed. Julian heard a promise said with no blame. Ivan refused to let one child's tears be outweighed. Frankl found meaning inside the camps, and Helen found a word at the pump. Not one of them asked anyone to prove their pain was big enough to count. Ranking doesn't make anyone's pain smaller. It just leaves someone alone with theirs.
screen: `JOB'S FRIENDS SAT, AND SAID NOTHING.` · `WEEP WITH, NOT WEIGH AGAINST.` · `LIKE A GAS, IT FILLS THE ROOM.` · `A WEEK WITH NO SCALE.` · then, large: `NO RANKING.`

segments.voice: Let something that hurts right now come to mind, big or small, and notice if a voice shows up to compare it: at least, others have it worse, I shouldn't. When it does, set the scale down and let your own thing be the size it is. Then, if you like, bring someone else who's hurting to mind, and let theirs be its size too: two pains side by side, neither one weighed.
No ranking. Pain kept company with, not weighed against anyone else's: weep with them that weep. Today's word.
Your line: weep with them that weep. The week held Shu, Julian, the question stays, meaning, Frankl, water, and no ranking. That's day seven hundred thirty-five, and a week.
